# Product wiki direction: strong thesis, dangerous breadth

## Judgement

**Verdict:** pursue a narrow pilot, not a company platform yet. The defensible promise is an evidence trail from *why* a product change exists to the task, scenario, code change and later drift, with a useful human page at each point. A git-backed wiki with an agent is not by itself a differentiator; fewer stale answers and faster safe changes would be.

**What is strong.** Decision [0017](docs/decisions/0017-product-wiki-as-source-of-truth.md) puts intent and work in one product-owned repository, separate from restricted code, and gives local and central users the same git truth. This can give people portable knowledge, reviewable history and exits from the service. Decisions [0003](docs/decisions/0003-federation-by-normalized-contract-ids.md) and [0004](docs/decisions/0004-source-agnostic-core-with-fact-plugins.md) give federation a concrete join key and require sources plus coverage, rather than pretending an AI has understood every repository. This is more useful than another chat over documents *if* the chain is accurate.

There is genuine leverage already: [src/model/schema.ts](src/model/schema.ts) defines scenarios, entities, evidence and contract-bearing interfaces; [src/check/model-check.ts](src/check/model-check.ts) checks evidence, stale blobs and scenario-to-requirement ids; [src/adapters/ladybug-engine.ts](src/adapters/ladybug-engine.ts) and [docs/system/capabilities/graph-queries.md](docs/system/capabilities/graph-queries.md) support time-filtered dependency queries. [src/wiki/build.ts](src/wiki/build.ts) builds static Starlight/Zensical pages with link checks, and [src/server/http.ts](src/server/http.ts) stores sent models and serves view text. These are foundations, **not** a writable product wiki or a code index. The accepted [wiki capability](docs/system/capabilities/wiki.md) still says a repository's `README.md` and `docs/` become read-only pages; the [server capability](docs/system/capabilities/server.md) explicitly has no authentication and never reads a repository.

**What could fail.** The biggest change is custody. Today's [model check](src/check/model-check.ts) assumes the model, evidence blobs, code and capability requirements are in *one* git repository; [0017](docs/decisions/0017-product-wiki-as-source-of-truth.md) separates them. Cross-repository pins, permission-aware references, links across rewritten history and missing code access all need real semantics. Also, [docs/vision.md](docs/vision.md) still excludes a wiki editor and calls the old installed contract the direction: it is not evidence that the new editor exists. The first milestone should explicitly replace those contracts, not silently promise both.

Non-engineers may prefer a familiar, forgiving editor to Markdown, branches and merges. A chat does not fix weak navigation, formatting, mobile access, rich tables or notification habits. Git excels at a modest number of durable reviewed changes, not multiple people editing the same paragraph, live comments and a commit per small chat turn; automatic rebase can alter the intended meaning, while a rejected push makes a successful-looking edit disappear. A revert creates a *new* commit; it is neither a guaranteed one-click reversal of dependent edits nor erasure of secrets or harmful text from git history.

An agent that applies without confirmation makes every prompt-injected document, ambiguous instruction and broad rewrite a production write request. Limit its tools, context, path set and transaction size; show the diff **after** a successful bounded commit with obvious undo, and escalate destructive, permission-changing and cross-page edits before executing them. A pretty diff is not sufficient if the commit is attributed to a human without a verifiable actor: git `author` is metadata, not authentication. Give people per-product roles, a server credential and an audit record for human/agent identity; authorize every read, query and write, including source snippets and cross-product graph traversals. Git history and indexes retain personal or confidential material even after page deletion; test deletion and redaction procedures before ingesting transcripts.

The current [server](docs/system/capabilities/server.md) is localhost/no-auth and accepts uploaded compiled models; central multi-tenant reading, auth, isolation and git-backed writes are new systems. The current [history store](src/adapters/sqlite-history.ts) is authoritative for received model assertions and LadybugDB is derived from it, not rebuilt directly from the product repo; [0017](docs/decisions/0017-product-wiki-as-source-of-truth.md) changes the source of truth. Specify what happens to recorded-time history on replay, force-push, bad commits and index lag. The many moving parts—editable wiki, agent runtime, permissions, git collaboration, skills/tracker migration, own code index, federation and company abstractions—are several products, not one two-week milestone. A single owner with agents still pays integration, operations and support costs.

**Competition.** Notion AI already edits workspace pages and searches connected tools, while Confluence AI/Rovo drafts content and can create Jira work; “chat next to a page” is not a moat ([Notion AI](https://www.notion.com/help/notion-ai-faqs), [Confluence AI](https://www.atlassian.com/software/confluence/ai)). More pointedly, [GitHub wikis](https://docs.github.com/en/communities/documenting-your-project-with-wikis/about-wikis) and [GitLab wikis](https://docs.gitlab.com/user/project/wiki/) are already separate Git repositories with browser editing, and GitHub/GitLab have issues and PR/MR links. [Backstage TechDocs](https://backstage.io/docs/features/techdocs/) publishes Markdown from code-adjacent repositories; [Linear Agent](https://linear.app/docs/linear-agent) creates and updates work. These are not proven equivalents to a checked intent→scenario→code→history graph, but madarch must compete on **trusted evidence and cross-product impact**, not storage format, basic editing or AI chat. Integrate with existing work systems before trying to replace their best workflows; actual substitution remains a pilot hypothesis.

### Assumptions worth trying to kill cheaply

| Assumption | Cheapest test and failure signal |
| --- | --- |
| A non-engineer will maintain the product source in this wiki | Give a PM and analyst each one real edit in a clickable page prototype, unassisted; observe completion time, errors and whether they return the next week. |
| A requirement-to-code link written at task launch is useful and stays honest | Trace one recent feature from requirement through a real task and PR; have a second engineer find the code without guidance. Flag links that have no reviewed code evidence. |
| One git repo handles team edit traffic | Simulate 10 editors on two different pages and the same page against a bare test remote; count retries, lost edits, elapsed save time, and legible conflict resolutions. |
| Instant agent commits are welcomed and reversible | Put a one-page, non-sensitive bounded agent edit in front of three users; log wrong changes, undo success, correction time and trust afterwards. No default access to broader pages. |
| Agents can use organisation models within budget | Meter tokens and spend for 20 real edit/comment requests; ask the budget owner for a per-team cap and a no-model fallback. |
| Per-product access can be enforced across wiki, snippets and graph | Threat-test a user with product A access but not product B against page search, graph traversal and agent context; any B content returned fails. |
| Contract ids can connect the team's actual repositories | Label ten real provider/consumer interfaces from two repos, compare normalized ids and explain unmatched ones; do not treat missing extraction coverage as absence ([0003](docs/decisions/0003-federation-by-normalized-contract-ids.md), [0004](docs/decisions/0004-source-agnostic-core-with-fact-plugins.md)). |
| A separate product repo can preserve evidence to code after movement | Move one real scenario/evidence chain from the old in-repo model to a pinned code ref; test rename, changed file, inaccessible repo and force-push. |
| The wiki can replace or coexist with the team's task tool | Run one real task in both places for a week; compare duplicate-entry time, missed updates and whether the team chooses the wiki next time. |

## Creative ideas

1. **[Quick win] A “why is this here?” button on each page and code-linked element.** Show the smallest chain from source quote or decision through requirement, scenario and task to a reviewed change, with the commit and evidence status. A newcomer gets an answer they can check instead of a generated paragraph.
2. **[Quick win] A change receipt rather than an AI summary.** Every agent edit gets an actor, base revision, paths, intent, validation result, diff and undo link on the page. A PM can inspect exactly what happened after an immediate change without understanding git.
3. **[Quick win] A landing page of unanswered decisions, not a generic dashboard.** Group broken citations, missing owners, unanswered comments and uncertain code links by the person who can resolve them. A team can spend ten minutes a week closing concrete knowledge gaps.
4. **[Quick win] “Is this still true?” on a requirement.** Show last edited time, last linked code change and index coverage side by side, explicitly “unknown” when code was not indexed. A product owner sees where to ask for review without mistaking freshness for correctness.
5. **[Quick win] Import as pointers, not migration.** Mirror a small read-only set of existing pages and tasks from the team's current tools, then invite editing only the three canonical pages needed for the pilot. People can try the new links without being forced to abandon familiar habits on day one.
6. **[Bet] Task launch as a trace envelope.** Starting work binds a task to requirement/scenario ids; the eventual PR and changed symbols enter a pending evidence list for human review. Engineers stop reconstructing “why” months later, while a task is never declared implemented merely because a file changed.
7. **[Bet] Drift as a question, not a red warning.** When code changes outside linked work, show candidate affected requirements with coverage and confidence, then ask the owner to link, amend or say unrelated. This can reveal undocumented change without turning every rename into a false alarm.
8. **[Bet] A contract boundary map with two-sided ownership.** For each normalized contract id, display provider, consumers, code refs, declared obligations and the last two teams to change it; preserve “unmatched” as a visible state. A cross-team change gets a contact and an impact path before release.
9. **[Bet] Rehearse a proposed change over a disposable graph.** Overlay a branch's code and a draft requirement, then list scenarios and dependent contracts that would change, with evidence and index gaps. Teams can discuss impact without publishing speculative assertions as truth.
10. **[Bet] Incident rewind with two clocks.** Compare what the team *believed then* against the code and deployments believed to be in use at the incident, and label the gaps. An on-call engineer can distinguish a stale model from a new regression; this depends on preserving valid and recorded time honestly.
11. **[Bet] A bounded assistant for structured edits.** Give the page chat a typed job such as “add an alternative flow to this scenario,” scoped to that page and known ids; reject references that do not resolve. Users get conversational editing without giving an agent arbitrary repository write rights.
12. **[Moonshot] Company-wide “who breaks if we retire this?”** Traverse product manifests and federated contract ids into ownership and business-use-case impact, with visibility filtered for the asking person. A platform team sees a defensible retirement plan rather than an organisation-wide hairball.
13. **[Moonshot] Reusable intent patterns across products.** A company-level abstraction could describe a common flow or policy once and show which product scenarios conform, diverge or have unknown coverage. It helps governance only after several products have proven the same vocabulary; do not start by inventing an ontology.

## The two-week first slice

Choose **one willing product team with one PM/analyst and one engineer**, one existing product, one code repository and one real change underway. Success at day 10: the PM can change a requirement without using git; the engineer can open its page and reach the scenario, task, accepted PR/commit and a pinned code file/line; both can see who changed it and undo a bounded bad edit. A newcomer can answer “why does this feature exist and where is it?” in five minutes, and at least two participants choose to use the wiki again unaided. Measure edit latency, conflict rate and agent cost, not just page views.

- **Days 1–2:** make a small separate product repository with a manifest pinning that code repo and three canonical pages: one requirement, one scenario, one active task. Reuse current model/schema and link checks where they fit; bridge the old in-repo evidence rather than claiming it is already portable. Keep the team's current task tool as an external link.
- **Days 3–7:** add one authenticated product-scoped write path for a Markdown page and a narrow page-chat instruction, both using the same validation and git commit transaction. Compare the client's base commit or blob before saving; different pages serialize cleanly, a same-page conflict is shown as a conflict, **never silently overwritten**. Commit with server identity plus verified human actor metadata, display the diff and provide revert with conflict checks. Rebuild the affected page promptly and the whole site asynchronously, showing last indexed commit.
- **Days 8–10:** run the real change through the wiki, have three people edit or review, exercise simultaneous edit and malicious page instruction, then inspect links and failures together. Stop or simplify if users cannot finish an edit, incorrect agent commits are hard to spot/undo, or evidence cannot survive the repo split. Keep a human-written fallback for a stalled agent.

**Leave out:** multi-product federation and company abstractions; automatic whole-code indexing, deep call/data flow and computed implementation status; full tracker/skill-set replacement; realtime co-editing; transcript ingestion; rich editing; unrestricted agent tools; public deployment/SSO and enterprise permission matrices. Do not expose this pilot to sensitive documents or other products. This slice tests [0017](docs/decisions/0017-product-wiki-as-source-of-truth.md)'s risky user/write path while using the accepted graph instead of rebuilding every layer at once.

## Questions before chartering, in order

1. **Who is the first real team, and what exact weekly job will they move?** If nobody volunteers a PM/analyst and a live change, start with a facilitated prototype, not infrastructure.
2. **Is the wiki replacing work tracking or linking to an existing tracker first?** Replacement requires lifecycle, notifications, permissions, reporting and skill-adapter migration; linking keeps the pilot small.
3. **What may the server agent commit without prior approval, and on whose authority?** Define path scope, action limits, destructive cases, audit identity, undo window and spending ceiling before a write API.
4. **Which documents and graph edges may each role read, including cross-product answers and source snippets?** Strict separation changes indexing and federation design; if all pilot content is public internally, say so explicitly but do not infer enterprise safety.
5. **What is a durable link to code when the wiki and code are different repositories?** Decide pinned refs, symbol/file anchors, force-push behavior and who confirms inferred links; this determines the graph schema and drift claims.
6. **Must two people edit the same page at the same time?** If yes, git per commit plus optimistic rejection may not meet the UX bar; test co-editing or reconsider the store. If no, conflict detection and a clear retry path are enough to start.
7. **Where do model calls run, who pays, and what happens offline or when the provider fails?** This changes the promise of “same locally and centrally” and whether a no-model editor is mandatory.
8. **What is the measurable reason to use this instead of the team's existing tools?** If traceability does not save real time or prevent a real mistake in the pilot, narrow the product to evidence/impact rather than building a general wiki.

**Source note:** The requested `README.md` is absent in this checkout; I used the named decisions, vision, glossary, capability specs and `src/` instead. The pre-existing working tree modification to `.beads/issues.jsonl` was not touched.

title: Pushes of tips whose tracker export exceeds execFileSync's 1 MB buffer are refused: the adapter's at-revision reads swallow ENOBUFS and report every task as missing
description:
Found 2026-10-11 ~19:00 MSK landing walk-fix #6 (a docs-only commit naming madarch-iuc.17) from a worktree off main 63b40eeb: the pre-push hook refused with 'task does not exist' for a task the tip export holds. Root cause: adapter.mjs readExport(rev) runs execFileSync('git', ['show', rev:path]) with no maxBuffer; node's default is 1 MiB and main's export is ~1.09 MB, so every at-revision read throws ENOBUFS, the bare catch returns '', and the commit-link check judges the commit against an empty tracker. The working-tree read (readFileSync) is unaffected, which is why pre-commit and the backlog gate stayed green while pre-push failed.

## Done when
adapter.mjs's execFileSync git calls carry an explicit maxBuffer (the 1<<28 check-commits already uses), a test covers an export above the old 1 MiB default read at a revision, and a push of a tip holding such an export passes the commit-link check.

## Falsified if
a push whose at-revision export is large is refused for a task the export holds.
close_reason: Fixed in 0eb59ecb: the adapter execFileSync git calls carry maxBuffer 1<<28 (the size check-commits already uses); a regression test reads this repository own export at HEAD; landed on main 1da0f27a, Product documents green.

title: Align the wiki and model-check capability specs with current behavior.
description:
Found during acceptance of `madarch-d7v3.2` at `e5d3840e`. The present-documents check passed with zero new errors but asked that `docs/system/capabilities/wiki.md` and `docs/system/capabilities/model-check.md` be read against the implementation. Searches found no open task covering these behavior claims.

## Findings

- `docs/system/capabilities/wiki.md:18-20` promises element descriptions when present, but the element schema has no `description` field (`src/model/schema.ts:70-85`, `src/model/compiled-schema.ts:165-183`) and the element-page builder does not render one (`src/wiki/pages.ts:314-330`).
- `docs/system/capabilities/wiki.md:65-70` claims both wiki engines produce the same pages, but Starlight refuses when document routes collide (`src/wiki/build.ts:346-354`); route normalization folds case, drops punctuation and trailing `index` (`src/wiki/starlight.ts:78-97`), with collision tests at `test/wiki-starlight.test.ts:104-120`.
- `docs/system/capabilities/model-check.md:143-147` describes instability/hub metrics as counting relations. The implementation counts distinct neighboring elements (`src/check/model-problems.ts:177-188, 211-223`).
- `docs/system/capabilities/model-check.md:187-190` omits warnings and notes from the report groups; both are emitted by `scripts/check-model.ts:62-69` and defined in `src/check/model-check.ts:41-59`.
- `docs/system/capabilities/model-check.md:155-158, 219-224` omits hidden-coupling limits: merge commits and commits touching more than 30 files are excluded (`src/check/model-check.ts:414-442`, threshold `src/check/model-problems.ts:43-48`), and shallow clones use only available history (`src/check/model-check.ts:655-662`).
- `docs/system/capabilities/model-check.md:177-180` says views use the checked revision's model. The check loads the model from the checkout (`src/check/model-check.ts:792`; `src/model/load.ts:412-453`); `--rev` supplies the revision for history/render time (`src/check/model-check.ts:875-877`).
- `docs/system/capabilities/model-check.md:118-125` does not distinguish the required `madarch/review.md` and `## Assignment` table from optional `## Claims`, or mention duplicate paths/table-shape errors (`src/check/model-check.ts:535-563, 857-865`; tests `test/model-check.test.ts:1640-1660, 1707-1725, 1973-2009`).

## Done when

- Both capability documents describe the current implementation accurately for these cases.
- The documentation check and a read-only review find no remaining mismatch in the listed claims.
- No runtime behavior changes are made by this documentation task.

Disproved if any listed claim still predicts a result different from the implementation or its tests.

## Left out

- Implementing unsupported runtime behavior (such as model element descriptions) to match the old wording.
- Unrelated capability-document drift.

## Budget

The standalone milestone's finding budget is fully used (7 of 7). This item is deferred while the owner decides whether it should wait for later or replace named planned work with an approved budget change. No scope change is approved here.

title: `madarch new` creates a draft product repository with its constitution, its manifest and its git history
description:
Outcome 1 of idea-to-wiki (charter docs/milestones/idea-to-wiki.md). Change `draft-product` (docs/changes/draft-product/change.md), capability product-repository.

A draft product repository is what a person with only an idea starts from: a real git repository holding the product's constitution, its manifest with a stable id, and the folders the wiki, the model, the skills and the prototypes live in. This stage delivers its creation and reading; the wiki that opens on it is stage 2.

## Done when

title: Repair the four madarch new tests that read the day in the test process zone, not the command s
description:
Found 2026-10-10 while closing madarch-rtr out: four tests in test/product-cli.test.ts fail on this machine between 21:00 and 24:00 UTC (00:00-03:00 MSK), and pass the rest of the day.

bun test runs the test file's own process in UTC whatever the machine's zone is (probed on bun 1.4.2: new Date().toString() inside bun test is GMT+0000 with TZ unset, and GMT+0300 for the same script outside it). The file's todayName() therefore reads the UTC day, while the child it spawns (bun scripts/madarch.ts new) inherits no TZ and reads the machine's local day, which is what the product's own rule uses (change draft-product, "The draft's name": idea-YYYY-MM-DD, of the day's date, from the local date). The two disagree whenever the local date differs from UTC's, so the assertion folder === idea-<todayName()> fails.

Evidence, this machine (TZ Europe/Moscow), 2026-10-09T21:27Z, on the landed revision 4be4f96:
MADARCH_SKIP_PERF=1 bun run test -> 1264 pass, 34 skip, 4 fail of 1302 tests across 58 files. All four are madarch new tests:
- test/product-cli.test.ts:172 expected /tmp/madarch-cli-elsewhere-m0HF4P/idea-2026-10-09, received /tmp/madarch-cli-elsewhere-m0HF4P/idea-2026-10-10
- test/product-cli.test.ts:184 (--home=FOLDER), :335 (--home with spaces) and the --home over MADARCH_HOME case, the same way.
CI is green on the same revision because GitHub's runners are UTC, where the two clocks agree.

## DONE WHEN
MADARCH_SKIP_PERF=1 bun run test is green on this machine at any hour: the command's child process is given the same zone the test file's own process reads, the test still asserts the rule (the day's local date), and the product's behaviour is unchanged.

title: Serve a product's wiki: its pages read from the working tree and the API the app reads
description:
Change `draft-product`, capability `product-wiki` (docs/changes/draft-product/capabilities/product-wiki.md), requirements `pages`, `live` and `result`; capability `server`, requirement `serves-wiki`.

Both halves of the read path, in one task:
- pages from the working tree: every Markdown file under the product's `docs/` and `README.md` at its root, ordered by code point of the path; a page's title is its first level-one heading, else its file's name without its extension; a page's text is read from disk on every call and never cached; the wiki's revision is a digest of the pages' paths and contents (so the same tree gives the same revision, and an unchanged wiki is never shown as changed); a path the wiki does not hold, and a path that climbs out of the product, are refused naming it;
- the server's product mode: `startServer` takes a product folder and/or a data folder, at least one, and offers each part's routes; `GET /api/product`, `GET /api/pages`, `GET /api/page?path=…`; the app's built files served from the app's folder; `index.html` for a path the app does not hold, so a page's address can be reloaded and linked; JSON refusals naming what was asked for; one log line per request carrying method, path, status and no document content. The server prints/returns the address it listens on, serves no wiki without a product folder, and refuses to start with neither.

Owned scope: `src/product-wiki/` (new), `src/server/wiki-app.ts` (new), `src/server/http.ts`, `src/index.ts`, and the test files for both halves. Tests go through the HTTP interface on a free port and through the page library, with fixture folders the tests create; the server's existing routes and their tests must keep passing.

## Done when
Tests show: the API lists the fixture's pages with their titles and the revision; a page's Markdown comes back whole; a missing page is refused with its path; a path under the app's routes answers `index.html`; the log line carries the method, path and status and no document text; asking twice after a file changes gives the new bytes; the product's files and git status are unchanged by every request. `bun run check` and the whole existing suite pass.

title: A task that spawns a long-running command and waits in its tests spends its session budget in those waits
description:
Found during the madarch-rtr run, 2026-10-09: task madarch-rtr.2.3 (the `madarch serve` wiring, one worker session) overran its 75-minute bound and was stopped with its work uncommitted and its own test file failing 6 of 18.

## What was measured
- The task bundled three mechanisms in one session: the wiki app built once on first use (its own toolchain and cache), the server started by a command that must keep running, and tests that spawn the real command and wait up to 20 seconds for it to serve.
- Its test file takes about two minutes per run, so the session's 75 minutes covered roughly twenty iterations, most of them waiting inside `whenServing` while the spawned command printed nothing and started no server.
- `bun run check` was clean and the sources were written when the bound tripped; only the spawned-command path never served.

## What it suggests
- A task whose tests spawn a long-running process and wait for a bounded timeout spends its budget in those waits: the task should either be split so the spawned-command path is its own task with a small test file, or name a much shorter wait and a smoke test beside the full one.
- A first-use build path (install and build a second toolchain inside the task's own checkout) is a task of its own when its failure mode is silent.

## Done when
The rule above is applied where it belongs (the task break-down or the brief), and a worker session that runs this shape of task finishes inside its bound, with a test that fails fast when the spawned command does not serve.

comments.text:
Decision 2026-10-10, by the closer at the feature's close-out: this finding stays open — it does not close with the run, and it is not this change's behaviour.

Why: its rule (a task whose tests spawn a long-running command waits in them; split the spawned-command path into its own task with a small test file and a short failing-fast wait, and never bundle a first-use build into it) applies to the planning of future runs, where there is nothing to apply it to today: the stage-2 tasks at 4be4f96 are done. It is genuinely new work on how tasks are briefed and sized, so it stays a finding in the milestone's queue, attached to this feature as its provenance. Whoever briefs the next run with a spawn-and-wait task or plans a first-use build should read it and its stage-2 measured numbers first.

The stage-2 test file since measures the spawned-command wait bounded (15 s in printedLiveFacts) — the failing-fast half of the rule exists; the task-shaping half still has no owner.

title: Decide whether the server needs a restartable query-engine process
description:
A decision the owner holds, for the server of this outcome: whether the query engine must run in a separate process restarted after N queries or M megabytes.

## Corrected 2026-09-25
This decision was filed on a stage-3 reviewer's single measurement that read as a LadybugDB defect: memory growing by about 85 KB per recursive query with a time filter, flat without it. Checked since, that reading is wrong. The filter clause makes no difference; the growth comes from our own configuration, with LadybugDB's default of one execution thread per core and a new statement prepared for every query time, and from synchronous test loops that never let the runtime release dropped statements. The measurements and the fix are in madarch-ti6.2.

## Affects
The server of this outcome, which runs for days. Not views, the agent skill, or the foundation's correctness.

## Recommendation
No restartable process. Once madarch-ti6.2 lands, its long-run test shows whether memory levels off; if it does, the server holds one engine for its lifetime, rebuilt only when the history changes, and this decision closes on that evidence. If it still grows, the restartable process (rebuilt from the history, which is fast and exact) is the fallback.

## Meanwhile
Nothing waits on this before the server is built; madarch-ti6.2's result releases it.
close_reason: Owner decision 2026-10-01: not needed; the in-process engine is bounded (ti6.2 long-run evidence), the update path debt is madarch-8iw

title: Bound the query engine's memory by limiting LadybugDB's threads and not preparing a statement per query time
description:
Found 2026-09-25 while checking the recorded cause behind the server's memory decision (madarch-ti6.1). Measured with LadybugDB 0.20.4 under Bun 1.4.2 and Node 26, on a 14-core machine, 10 000 to 40 000 queries per run.

## What was measured
- The filter clause in a recursive query is not the cause: with and without it, memory grows the same and levels off (about 115 MB for 30 000 queries of a 200-node chain returning a count).
- Returning the path's relations (`rels(p)`, with or without `list_transform`) costs memory per execution thread. At the default thread count (one per core, 14 here) a process running `dependents` settles between 0.7 and 1.2 GB for a 50-element graph; with 1 or 2 threads (`new Connection(db, n)` or `setMaxNumThreadForExec`) it settles near 170 to 250 MB, and each query is about twice as fast (2.3 ms against 5.4 ms).
- `dependencyQuery` writes `valid`/`known` into the statement text (LadybugDB refuses `$parameters` inside a recursive relationship filter: "Cannot evaluate $_ because it does not depend on n or r", tried in five forms). A caller asking "now" through an advancing clock therefore prepares a new statement on every call: our engine at 2 threads, fixed time, stays at 253 MB over 40 000 calls; with an advancing time it climbs towards 1 GB.
- A prepared statement dropped by our code is released only when Node or Bun run its native finalizer, after garbage collection and an event-loop turn. A synchronous loop that never yields fills the 256 MB buffer pool within 10 000 distinct statements; with a yield every 500 calls 40 000 distinct statements plateau near 340 MB, under both runtimes. This is not a LadybugDB defect, and a server yields between requests.

## Done when
- the engine's connection runs with a small fixed number of threads (1 or 2, chosen by measurement);
- a query's `valid`/`known` are reduced to the latest time in the model history at or before them (the answer can change only at those times), so the statement texts are bounded by the history's size and the prepared-statement cache hits; the graph-queries conformance tests pass unchanged;
- a long-run test (at least 20 000 `dependents` and `view` calls with an advancing clock, yielding to the event loop between batches) shows memory levelling off under a stated bound, and is skipped with the other performance tests under `MADARCH_SKIP_PERF`;
- the code's statements that blamed LadybugDB are corrected: the engine's comments that a prepared statement is "never freed" and the B1 stability test's explanation of its growth (decision 0009 and `docs/system/index.md` were corrected when this was filed), and `docs/system/index.md`'s known unknown is updated to the measured result;
- an issue asking LadybugDB to accept parameters inside recursive relationship filters is drafted and shown to the owner; it is sent only with their yes.

## Left out
A worker process restarted after N queries (the open decision madarch-ti6.1 waits on this measurement); replacing the Node binding (the C API through Bun's FFI or the WASM build: both cost more and change nothing measured here).

title: Bound the query engine's memory for a server that runs for days
description:
Stage 1 of madarch-ti6 (change server-views). The query engine runs with a small fixed number of execution threads and prepares statements only for the history's own times, and a long-run test shows its memory levelling off. Its result decides madarch-ti6.1.

## Done when
madarch-ti6.2's criteria hold on the assembled revision: the graph-queries conformance tests pass unchanged; the long-run test (at least 20 000 dependents and view calls with an advancing clock, yielding between batches) levels off under its stated bound and is skipped under MADARCH_SKIP_PERF; the statements blaming LadybugDB are corrected; the LadybugDB issue draft is shown to the owner. Seen by: the long-run test's printed memory curve (internal: a person sees nothing else).

title: Report architecture problems as the server's own checks on the graph
description:
Idea from the 2026-09-27 planning of madarch-utk. The local model check (madarch-utk.1) computes, for one repository, dependency cycles, unstable dependencies, hubs, magic sources and sinks, trust-boundary crossings and hidden coupling, each with its method (Martin's ADP and SDP, Arcan, Microsoft's STRIDE rules for data flow diagrams, Mo, Cai, Kazman and Xiao's modularity violation). The vision's 'Checks' asks for rule violations and drift across the whole graph.

The idea: the same problems, plus elements nothing depends on (zombies) and co-change scatter (D'Ambros et al.), evaluated by the server on the whole graph across repositories, as history queries and on a pull request's what-if overlay (madarch-c70), reusing the local check's code.

Would show it is worth it: findings that only appear across repositories (a cycle through two services in different repositories).
Left out: code-level analysis (complexity, duplication, ownership), which madarch consumes from other tools.

title: A malformed agent answer fails one unit with its reason and is retried with the validation error, instead of blocking the whole fill
description:
Found by the first real checkpoint run (omp, GLM 5.3 flash, training repository, 2026-10-17 16:38 MSK): the first claims call returned an answer whose sourceIds was not an array; the run printed 'Agent output field sourceIds must be an array' and stayed blocked with the unit 'running'.

## DONE WHEN
- Agent output is parsed tolerantly where meaning is unambiguous (a single id string becomes a one-element list; JSON inside a fenced block is found) and strictly otherwise.
- An invalid answer is retried up to twice with the exact validation errors fed back to the agent; after that the unit is failed with the errors and the raw answer saved, the run goes on with the units that do not depend on it, and the run's report names it.
- A unit left 'running' by a crashed process is requeued on the next start (the runtime's rule) — verified by a test.
- Tests with recorded malformed answers.

title: madarch fill cannot claim a repository of madarch's own size: the claims call embeds the whole source tree in one argv entry and exec refuses with E2BIG
description:
madarch fill cannot extract claims from a repository of madarch's own size: the one claims call embeds the whole source tree in one argv entry, and exec refuses with E2BIG

## What a person does
In a fresh clone of madarch (origin/main 64fa1a7f), run the fill of a product around it exactly as docs/changes/fill-pipeline-monday/checkpoint-2.md sets up (omp, glm-5.3 flash, wrapper teeing calls; caps 150 calls / 90 minutes, the walk's owner authorization on madarch-tzte.11).

## What happens
The run completes inventory and all 318 deterministic index units, then the claims unit fails and the run blocks: `E2BIG: argument list too long, posix_spawn <omp wrapper>` (measured 2026-10-17, two starts 21:09 and 21:11 UTC; the second start resumed the same fill chain and blocked identically, so the block is deterministic, not load). Not one omp call is ever spawned (the wrapper tee recorded zero call streams; the budget still counted 2 dispatches).

## Why (evidence, file:line:full path)
- src/product/fill.ts:114 (`the claims prompt`) strings together repository-claims.md, the registry, `JSON.stringify(allSources)` and the inline materials. `allSources` (src/product/fill.ts:93) carries the full text of every file in the pinned tree: for madarch at 64fa1a7f that is 943 files / 10,674,715 blob bytes plus materials — about 10.7 MB in one argument.
- src/product/fill-agents.ts:56 (spawn) and src/product/fill-agents.ts:24 (agentCommand) pass the prompt as the last argv entry. Linux refuses any single argv or env string above MAX_ARG_STRLEN 131072 bytes, and this machine's ARG_MAX is 2097152 (getconf).
- The training-repository checkpoints (checkpoint-1.md, checkpoint-2.md) never met this because that repository is ~50 KB of sources. No chunking, per-file claims units or stdin prompt path exists anywhere in src/product/ (grep for chunk|E2BIG|stdin over src/product, 2026-10-17).

## What should happen
The fill must be able to claim a repository whatever its size: the claims call needs a bounded prompt path (chunked claims units or a file/stdin-streamed prompt), and a prompt that exceeds the OS argv limit must fail the unit with a named, actionable outcome, not a bare posix_spawn error. To its own checkout is exactly the milestone's walk (docs/milestones/self-filling.md, "The walk"), so until this is fixed the success signal cannot be met.

## What disproves
A fill of the same product and snapshot completes claims and synthesis without E2BIG.

## Disproven requirement
docs/changes/fill-pipeline-monday/checkpoint-2.md verdict: with the fixes landed, one more short run against this same product finishes synthesis — scaling from the training repository to the walk's repository was never exercised.
close_reason: Superseded by decisions 0026/0027: no file content goes into prompts; claims become bounded graph-reading units (stage madarch-tzte.24).

Stage madarch-tzte.19 — "The fill runs on madarch's orchestrator: declared stages, persisted state machines, pg-boss, crash-safe" — accepted by the coordinator on 2026-10-19 on the assembled revision 8d72414613de4f7683d11ce4c4583b3251b4234e (branch chore/madarch-accept-stage-19, PR https://github.com/shady2k/madarch/pull/89 (opened; the coordinator merges nothing, the owner does)). Included tasks, each merged and recorded as implemented:
- madarch-tzte.19.1 — one database owner per process for the fact log, the query projection, the queue's tables and the orchestrator's (PR #75, merge 87a94e76).
- madarch-tzte.19.2 — the durable queue on pg-boss inside that owner (PR #79, merge fc76c4bd), and the queue's enqueue order inside one clock tick (PR #81, merge 5c712dea).
- madarch-tzte.19.3 — the declared stage registry and the stage graph derived from the declared capabilities (PR #74, merge 4161d38d).
- madarch-tzte.19.4 — the unit, run and chain state machines, pure tables persisted through the store with fencing tokens (PR #72, merge 6937ea0a).
- madarch-tzte.19.5 — the orchestrator: planning from the registry, admission within the run's limits, leases, splits, joins, staleness, cancellation and one publication per unit generation (PRs #82 and #83, merges 11c4bdda and cec43195).
- madarch-tzte.19.6 — the crash-injection suite over the compiled binary (PR #87, merge f2268254).
The acceptance review of that assembled revision returned fix-before-ship; its two blockers and two notes were fixed in a further commit (7df35bdc3038db97601f62a8d164aa4185a72fcc, PR ...) and a second review round answered ship. The accepted revision is the branch tip that carries both.

Criteria — the stage's DONE WHEN, clause by clause, on 8d72414613de4f7683d11ce4c4583b3251b4234e:
- "a crash-injection run of the compiled binary with fake stages and fake agents (extractor → splitting unit → child summaries → parent join → consumer)": test/fill-crash-suite.test.ts drives the compiled binary (test/fill-crash-fixture.ts builds it with `bun build --compile`) through the daemon service; its last test, "the packaged binary drives one run through the daemon service to its end", is the packaged walk, and "plans the three stages in the derived order and drives every unit to one publication" is the extractor → split → children → join → consumer chain.
- "on persistent PGlite": the same file, 11 tests, all passing on the pod (11 tests, 11 pass 0 fail, exit 0, 82 s in that run and 74-82 s alone; its own log line in the group run of 20261019-011119).
- "and on PostgreSQL with several executor processes": test/fill-crash-postgres.test.ts, 6 tests — three executors driving one chain, the run's own slots held across three executors, a claim a killed worker held recovered, a split killed before its acknowledgement, a worker that lost its fence publishing nothing, a disabled producer blocking with its starvation path. It needs MADARCH_TEST_POSTGRES_URL, which CI's checks job sets for its PostgreSQL service: the checks job of CI run 39171437383 passed on the tree, and its step is `bun test test/fill-crash-postgres.test.ts` with the pgvector service; a SkyPilot pod carries no PostgreSQL, so that leg is CI's alone.
- "one publication per unit generation": the crash suite's claim/publication/acknowledgement kills and its repeated request, plus "a published generation is an immutable record: a later job for it changes nothing" and the publication tests in test/fill-orchestrator.test.ts ("the same digest answers the existing record, and a different digest is refused"; "the facts, the state and the queue's settlement are one transaction: a failure rolls back all of them").
- "no lost children": test/fill-crash-suite.test.ts, "around the split: the sealed children stand, and the parent joins them after the restart"; the children and the parent's checkpoint are written in one transaction ("seals the children and the parent in one transaction, then joins the parent once they are published and fresh"), and the join reads the sealed generations ("a parent joins only while every child it sealed is still fresh").
- "barrier recovery": the same split test and the PostgreSQL leg's "a split killed before its acknowledgement loses no child and the parent joins them".
- "stale fences refused": the unit machine's own rules (test/fill-fsm.test.ts: "every worker step names its generation as well as its token, and no lease token is reused"; "the run's own sweep reports a lapsed lease with no token, and a worker's retry with its own"; the refusal table's late-token entries), the orchestrator's publication fence (test/fill-orchestrator.test.ts), and the PostgreSQL leg's "a worker that lost its fence publishes nothing" — the unit machine's token rules (test/fill-fsm.test.ts, "every worker step names its generation as well as its token, and no lease token is reused", "a late worker names an older fencing token than the unit holds", and the retries fenced by this acceptance's fix), and the PostgreSQL leg's "a worker that lost its fence publishes nothing".
- "concurrency enforced": test/fill-orchestrator.test.ts, "takes the run's slots and each stage's concurrency, in the order the plan named the units" and "a unit that waited climbs one place per ageing step, never past its stage's own order", beside the registry's own `concurrency` limits; and the PostgreSQL leg's "the run's own slots hold across three executors".
- "eventual recovery after kills around claim/split/publication/ack": the crash suite's four kill points: "around the claim: nothing is leased, and the run recovers and publishes once", "around the split", "inside the publication: the transaction rolls back and the retry publishes exactly once", "around the acknowledgement: the publication stands, and a repeated request answers it". The recovery requirement those kills exposed is now in the current specification (docs/system/capabilities/fill-orchestrator.md, "recovery").
- "an explicit starvation diagnostic when a required producer is disabled": test/fill-crash-suite.test.ts, "a disabled producer blocks the run and names the path that starves the consumer", test/fill-orchestrator.test.ts, "a required capability no enabled stage produces blocks the run with its starvation path" and "a producer the product disabled is named as the path, and nothing is planned", and the registry's own starvation tests ("planning reports what starves a stage, by its exact path").

Checks the revision owes; one receipt for each, on each of the six tasks, bound to content:REVISION (static to check:STATIC_REVISION):
- static: `bun run check` (tsc --noEmit, TypeScript 7.0.2) exit 0 on the accepted tree, run by the coordinator; CI's checks job ran the same command green on 7df35bdc.

comments.text:
[note from madarch-tzte.19.4] The fill state machines and their persistence are in src/fill/fsm-core.ts (the declared transition layer over XState's pure transition), src/fill/fsm.ts (the unit, run and chain tables, guards, actions and the unit Mermaid diagram) and src/fill/state-store.ts (six tables: fill_chain, fill_run, fill_unit, fill_unit_generation, fill_unit_lease, fill_transition).

What this task leaves for madarch-tzte.19.5:
1. The store borrows the database through one interface, FillStateDatabase = { transaction('snapshot' | 'write', (executor: SqlExecutor) => Promise<T>) }, which madarch-tzte.19.1's one owner per process must satisfy. test/fill-fsm-pglite.ts opens its own PGlite for the store's tests only: switch state-store.ts to the owner and delete that test adapter.
2. Every step returns its named effects for this task to perform after the new state is committed: enqueue-ready, revoke-lease, schedule-retry, suspend-parent, resume-join, record-draft, record-validation, record-publication, retract-draft, revoke-authority, record-resolution, emit-progress. Publication itself -- the uniquely constrained record, same-digest replay, different-digest refusal, revalidating recorded reads -- is this task's; the store only records the state, published_at and the journal row.
3. A generation's fence column is the authority. leaseUnit takes fence = current + 1 and attempt = current + 1; every worker step names its token and the fence-current guard refuses an older one with a named refusal (fill-unit/guard-refused, guard "fence-current"). A refused step writes nothing.
4. replaceStaleGeneration opens generation n+1 only from a stale generation, and only the generation its invalidation named; a cancelled or failed generation stays as its record.
5. The unit machine is tested against a hand-written expectation list of all 40 allowed transitions taken from decision 0027, every state and event pair the decision does not allow, every guard's refusal, and the diagram in the module doc comment is rendered from the same table by a test. Change record: docs/changes/madarch-fill-fsm/change.md.

title: A split whose suspension the machine refuses has already sealed its children, so a parent can stand without the children it sealed for
description:
Found by the independent review of madarch-tzte.19.7 (2026-10-19), while fixing the
claim a refused step left standing. Filed deferred: the `self-filling` milestone's
finding budget is far past its 8, so the choice of when to pay for this is the owner's.

## What happens
`src/fill/orchestrator.ts`'s `splitAttempt` seals a split in one transaction: it creates
the child units (`createUnitIn`), records their plan rows (`recordUnitPlanIn`), writes the
seal (`sealSplitIn`) and then takes the machine's `wait-for-children` step
(`advanceUnitIn`) — in that order, so the step's event can name the generations the store
just gave the children. A step the table refuses is a value, not a throw
(`src/fill/state-store.ts`), so the transaction commits the children and the seal row
while the parent stays where it was: a parent can stand `retry_wait` (or any other state)
without the children it sealed, and can later publish facts that never stood on them.
Decision 0027's split requirement is the invariant this breaks: "a parent waits for
exactly the children that were sealed with it or for none of them".

The window opens when the attempt's lease lapses under it while the stage still runs — the
run's own sweep retries the generation, the stage then returns `outcome: 'split'`, and the
step after the seal is refused. `test/fill-orchestrator.test.ts`'s "a split whose
suspension the machine refuses ends its claim" drives exactly that today and records the
sealed children as the state that follows, which is what this issue is about.

Impact today is small: a stage that splits again on its retry converges (`createUnitIn`
returns the standing children, the seal upserts, the parent waits), and no shipped stage
returns `outcome: 'split'` yet. A stage that decides differently on its retry — the stage
contract carries no attempt number, so its own graph read decides — publishes without its
children.

## Done when
- The children and the seal of a split stand only if the parent's `wait-for-children` step
  was allowed: judge the step before anything is inserted (its `children-sealed` guard
  reads the event, not the store, so a provisional child set is enough), or let the
  transaction roll back when the step is refused, and
- a test holds it: the refusal leaves no child unit, no seal row and no plan row for the
  split, and the retry that follows seals what it names.

## Evidence
- `src/fill/orchestrator.ts` `splitAttempt` (the seal transaction), `src/fill/fsm.ts`
  `children-sealed` (line 228), `docs/system/capabilities/fill-orchestrator.md`, "split".
- The review of madarch-tzte.19.7 (/tmp/review-19-7.log on the worker's machine) named it
  as its first should-fix.

Inputs are hashed from pinned repo tree/files, registry and upstream unit outputs. Stage boundaries recheck the default branch; only units whose declared inputs changed become stale. Stage madarch-tzte.20 — "Facts of code live in the product graph: schema, unit-scoped publication, bounded reads with tracked dependencies, checked writes" — accepted by the coordinator on 2026-10-19 on the assembled revision a63dee7b1713066b3fe99ead943d1a6f9b815892 (branch chore/madarch-accept-stage-20, based on origin/main 9ebd24b6; https://github.com/shady2k/madarch/pull/95 (opened; the coordinator merges nothing, the owner does)). The stage builds stage 2 of decision 0026, which the owner agreed point by point («Да», 2026-10-18, docs/decisions/0026-graph-first-fill.md), under decision 0027's storage, publication and staleness rules. All four changes are kind `no-behavior`, which the document policy does not require approval for (`approvalFor: ["behavior"]` in .shady2k/documents.json); none of them decides anything 0026 or 0027 do not, so no `approval:` record is posted and nothing is listed for the owner to decide beyond the two findings named below.

Included tasks, each merged and recorded as implemented:
- madarch-tzte.20.1 — the fill's code-fact schema: kinds, stages, provenance, layer, status, one version a kind, content-addressed ids and the check that names every reason a row is not a fact (PR #73, merge cc22c733).
- madarch-tzte.20.2 — the fact store through the one database owner: one row per content-addressed id, holdings per publishing unit, a publication replacing only its own unit's facts inside its own transaction, a draft readable as draft (PR #86, merge 2f879579).
- madarch-tzte.20.3 — the six bounded graph reads with 0026's caps and a marker that names every cut, and every read recorded as the reading unit's dependency (PR #92, merge d753b8fc).
- madarch-tzte.20.4 — the four checked write tools: the schema, the cited bytes read at the pinned commit, the referenced nodes, the unit's scope, and the draft set the machine records (PR #90, merge 089ec82d).

Criteria — the stage's DONE WHEN, clause by clause, on the accepted tree (the four modules and their four test files are byte-identical between d753b8fc and 9ebd24b6, so each merge's own CI stands for the code accepted here):
- "A code-fact schema (own namespace, stable content-addressed ids, no run ids) is stored through the single database owner; a unit's publication replaces only its own facts."
  The schema is `src/fill/facts.ts`: 25 node kinds and 15 edge kinds, each with its stages, provenance, layer, status, place rule and version; an id is the digest of the kind's declared identity and of nothing else (`factId`, `identityOfKind`), every path is a repository path, and `checkFact` names every reason a row is not a fact. `test/fill-facts.test.ts` holds it: 102 tests, including "the same fact gives the same id twice", "the same file read in two checkouts on two machines is one fact and one id", "a rerun at another commit, with another reader version and other counts, is the same fact", "no identity of any kind names a run, a unit, an attempt, a generation, a session or a time", and "every kind has a sample, so no kind is left untested".
  The store is `src/fill/fact-store.ts`: `fill_fact` (one row per id) and `fill_fact_holding` (one row per fact and publishing unit), created with the fill's other tables by `createFactStoreSchema` and written inside the executor the publication was given, so the facts, the generation's state, the queue's settlement and the publication record are one transaction. `test/fill-fact-store.test.ts` (PGlite, 25 tests) and `test/fill-fact-store-postgres.test.ts` (the same scenario and the same expectations on the server CI's checks job starts, 23 tests) hold "a unit's publication replaces only its own facts", "a fact two units publish keeps one row, with both publishers named in code point order", "a fact another unit still holds keeps its row and loses only the publisher that dropped it", "a retracted draft leaves nothing" and "a fact another unit is publishing is not swept away".
- "describe_scope, neighbors, references, claims_about, coverage, evidence_span answer within their size caps with truncation markers, and every read is recorded as the reader's dependency (query membership, empty results included)."
  `src/fill/graph-reads.ts` answers the six tools over the store's own rows and, for a span, the pinned commit's bytes; the caps are 0026's 8K tokens and about 200 lines (`DEFAULT_GRAPH_READ_LIMITS`), the estimate is one token per four code points, and the cap is the whole answer (its envelope reserved before the rows are bounded). `test/fill-graph-reads.test.ts` (28 tests) holds "a symbol with three callers answers those three, sorted by code point, untruncated", "an answer the cap cuts says so, and names how many rows were cut", "a row too large for the cap leaves the answer with none of them and a marker that says so", "a span longer than the cap is answered with the lines that fit and a marker naming the cut", and "every read is the reading unit's dependency: the reads are recorded with their memberships, an empty answer included, and a later publication that changes one marks the unit stale" — the last one against the orchestrator's own staleness sweep.
- "Checked writes (schema, cited bytes read by madarch at the pinned commit, referenced nodes, scope) land in a unit's draft set visible as draft and are published or retracted whole."
  `src/fill/checked-writes.ts` makes the four checks in order — the request's shape, the place (the scope, the pinned repository, the file in the commit's tree and the span inside the bytes), `checkFact`, the referenced nodes and the kinds their edge joins — and appends an accepted write to the unit's draft set; a refusal is a value carrying every reason at its field, its file and its line. `test/fill-checked-writes.test.ts` (21 tests) holds the task's two normal cases ("a fact citing lines 3-5 of a file that holds them lands in the unit's draft set, visible as draft"; "the same fact citing line 900 of a 10-line file is refused, and the refusal names the span"), the scope, a node the graph does not hold, an entity proposal's similar entities under their cap, and the publication of a unit's own checked writes through the machine's store.

title: Published facts are stored through the one database owner, a unit's publication replacing only its own facts
description:
Stage 2 of decision 0026: facts stored through the one database owner.

## DONE WHEN
- A fact store (tables through `src/adapters/database-owner.ts`) implements the orchestrator's sink for a published fact set (madarch-tzte.19.5's host interface): a unit's publication replaces only that unit's own facts in one transaction; a retracted draft leaves nothing; a fact two units publish keeps one row with both publishers, removed only when neither holds it.
- Draft sets are readable as draft by other units and never mixed with published facts. Normally publishing a unit's three facts then republishing two of them leaves exactly those two for that unit.
- Runs on PGlite and on PostgreSQL (the CI checks job has a server).

title: The bounded graph reads answer within their caps and record every read as the reader's dependency
description:
Stage 2 of decision 0026: bounded reads with tracked dependencies.

- `describe_scope`, `neighbors`, `references`, `claims_about`, `coverage` and `evidence_span` answer from the fact store within 0026's caps (tool answers at most 8K tokens, evidence spans about 200 lines), with a truncation marker naming what was cut.
- Every read is recorded as the reading unit's dependency: the query and its result membership, an empty result included; a later publication that changes that membership marks the unit stale (asserted with the orchestrator's staleness).
- Normally `neighbors` of a symbol with three callers answers those three, sorted by code point, untruncated.

title: Checked writes land in a unit's draft set only after the schema, the cited bytes, the referenced nodes and the scope are checked
description:
Stage 2 of decision 0026: checked writes into a unit's draft set.

## DONE WHEN
- `assert_fact`, `propose_entity`, `link` and `raise_question` check each write at once: the schema (`checkFact`), the cited bytes exist and are read by madarch at the pinned commit, referenced nodes exist, the write lies in the unit's scope; a refused write names the field and the reason.
- An accepted write lands in the unit's draft set, visible as draft; `propose_entity` answers with similar existing entities. Normally a fact citing lines 3–5 of a file that has them is accepted and visible as draft, and the same fact citing line 900 of a 10-line file is refused naming the span.

title: The deterministic stages fill the current madarch tree inside a 4 GB pod, the embedded store growing in proportion to the facts it holds
description:
Defect against stage madarch-tzte.21's DONE WHEN ("fill the graph for any repository size"), found by madarch-tzte.21.8's walk 2026-10-19.

## What happens
The deterministic stages over the current madarch tree (1090 tracked files, about 2800 units) grow the embedded PGlite store to about 1 GB (550 MB of tables, 475 MB of WAL), and the 4 GB pod kills the process (exit 137) twice; a 789-file tree reached 603 MB and was killed too. The walk could only be made on an older commit of 194 files (529 units, 84 s, store far smaller). A person's laptop runs the same PGlite store, so this is the product's limit, not the pod's.

## Done when
- The cause is measured and named (per-fact row size and indexes, the draft/publication double write, unchecked WAL growth, one transaction per unit holding everything, facts duplicated per publisher, occurrences dominating), with the store's size per kind before and after.
- Fixed at the cause so the deterministic stages over the current madarch tree complete on a 2 CPU / 4 GB pod, with the store's peak size and the process's peak memory recorded (target: store well under the tree's own size times a small factor; memory inside the pod with headroom).
- A test guards the fix (e.g. WAL is checkpointed or bounded during a run; a publication does not keep both draft and published copies), and the walk's numbers for the current tree are recorded in the change record.

Disproved by: a fill of the current madarch tree killed for memory on a 4 GB pod, or a store that grows without bound with the run.

title: The history stage writes the pinned commit's ancestry as commit facts and the task keys its messages name
description:

## DONE WHEN

- Incremental: a second run after one new commit writes only that commit's facts. Normally the first run on a throwaway repository of three commits writes exactly three commit facts in parent order.
- A shallow clone or a missing parent is reported as coverage, never a silent shorter history.
- Tests run the stage through `plan`/`execute` with a fake context on repositories the test makes; no outside repository. It reads Git directly (git log at the pinned commit); it does not need the snapshot reader.

title: The syntax stage writes each source file's symbols, definitions, comments, imports and entry points from tree-sitter
description:
Stage 3 of decision 0026, stage 3 syntax (tree-sitter, per file).

## DONE WHEN
- A registered stage `syntax` plans one unit per source file and writes `symbol`, `occurrence` (definitions), `comment`, `entry-point` and `test` facts and `contains`, `defines` and `import` edges for TypeScript, TSX, JavaScript and Go, reusing the grammars and walk of `src/product/fill-index.ts` where they fit.
- Each fact carries its place (repository path, byte and line span) and an id from `src/fill/facts.ts`; a file in a language without a grammar is coverage "not parsed", never dropped silently.
- Incremental: a file whose blob id did not change is not re-planned. Normally a fixture file with two exported functions and one import yields exactly those two symbols, their definitions and the import edge.
- The per-file extraction is a pure function of (repository path, bytes); the stage reads bytes through `SnapshotReader` (`src/fill/snapshot.ts`, the snapshot/inventory task) — write the pure part and its tests first, then the stage over the reader once that task lands.
- Wiki-build tests are not involved; the stage's own tests run on the pod (tree-sitter needs `--avx2`).

Decision recorded for madarch-tzte.21.5 (worker), 2026-10-18: a lock file is read by nothing in this task.

The coordinator's own words: "Lock files: read none for edges in this task."

What it narrows: the DONE WHEN's "package facts and dependency edges from package.json/bun.lock, go.mod and Cargo.toml" is read as the npm/bun ecosystem's package.json, the go.mod and the Cargo.toml. A bun.lock (or any other lock file) is a manifest of the stage's own set, so it has a unit, and that unit publishes one coverage gap naming that no fact of this stage carries a resolved version — a declared gap, never a silent skip.

Why: a dependency edge carries from/to/basis and no version, and an edge's ends must be nodes the graph holds (0026), so a lock file's resolved versions and the registry packages they name have no node here and no fact of this stage.

title: The syntax stage re-reads a file whose published import edge or coverage gap its specifiers no longer name
description:
A finding of the semantic resolution stage's review (madarch-tzte.21.6), out of that task's scope.

## Observed
`src/fill/stages/syntax.ts`'s plan re-reads a file only when its blob moved. Two of its published facts therefore keep an older answer after another stage has made them stale:
- a specifier it could not tie to a file is a coverage gap that never goes away once a file appears under it, even though stage 4 now resolves that specifier and writes the edges for it;
- an `import` edge it wrote keeps naming the file the specifier resolved to, when a file appears beside that target and the specifier now answers the new one (`./x.js` written beside the `x.ts` it resolved to).

Stage 4's plan (madarch-tzte.21.6) reads those two facts for its own incrementality and is bounded against them by its own coverage, so its edges end up newer than stage 3's gap and edge — the graph holds both answers.

## Done when
- stage 3's plan re-reads a file whose published coverage gap or `import` edge no longer matches what its specifiers name at the pinned commit (the same two rules stage 4's plan applies, one helper both plans call).
- A second run of an unchanged commit plans nothing in either stage, with a test for each.
- The change record of whichever task lands it says which older answer it retires.

    npm install -g --prefix ~/.local @agentclientprotocol/claude-agent-acp@0.93.0 @agentclientprotocol/codex-acp@2.2.2

- run 2026-10-19T06:55:13Z → 06:56:34Z (1 min 21 s of wall clock), `npm install` reported "added 133 packages in 1m", exit 0; npm 11.19.0, node v24.21.0.

## 2. The probe finds both connected (`bun scripts/madarch.ts fill --probe-acp`)

Two runs, both exit 0: the readable report at 06:57:58Z (2.2 s end to end, the run quoted here) and the same probe with `--json` at 2026-10-19T07:00:25.525Z, whose record the table's fields come from.

| pi | not installed | — | — | — | — |

"as before" for omp: the same finding and the same evidence line 22.1 recorded. pi stays not installed; this walk installed no `pi-acp`. The probe sends no prompt and installs nothing, so it spent no tokens.

## 3. One session and one prompt per agent, through madarch's own client (src/fill/acp.ts)

One scratch script outside the repository (in /tmp, not committed) called `connectAcpAgent` → `initialize()` → `newSession({cwd})` (no MCP server: this walk sends a prompt, not a unit) → **one** `session.prompt("Reply with the single word OK.")` → `session.usage()` → `connection.close()`. One attempt per agent: no retry, and no transport error to retry on.

**Claude Code** — start 06:58:30Z, record at 06:58:37.531Z, 7 184 ms in all.
- initialize 324 ms (protocol 1); `session/new` 1 200 ms; the prompt turn 5 624 ms; close 25 ms.
- updates streamed, in order: `available_commands_update`, `available_commands_update`, `usage_update` (context 21 845 / 1 000 000), `agent_message_chunk: "OK"`, `usage_update`.
- stop reason `end_turn`; answer **"OK"**.
- usage, as the agent reported it: input 2, output 4, total 21845, cache read 8607, cache write 13232; context 21 845 of 1 000 000 tokens.

**Codex** — start 06:58:51Z, record at 06:59:00.621Z, 8 303 ms in all.
- initialize 274 ms (protocol 1, auth methods api-key and chat-gpt, neither needed: the codex CLI on this machine is already logged in); `session/new` 2 844 ms; the prompt turn 5 159 ms; close 15 ms.
- updates streamed, in order: `available_commands_update`, an update of a kind madarch keeps as `other`, `agent_message_chunk: "OK"`, `usage_update` (context 17 745 / 475 000), two further `other` updates.
- stop reason `end_turn`; answer **"OK"**.
- usage, as the agent reported it: input 5452, output 5, total 17745, thought 0, cache read 12288, cache write 0; context 17 745 of 475 000 tokens.

Both agents reported usage, so neither needed the "not reported" path. Each session was closed, and the client signals the agent's whole process group on close: right after both walks, `ps` found no process running from `node_modules/@agentclientprotocol` — no adapter, no agent helper left behind (the three `claude --resume` processes on the machine belong to sessions started about 23 hours earlier).

The probe's catalogue reports an install's size as the package's own `dist.unpackedSize` (Claude Code 1 956 577 B ≈ 1.9 MiB, Codex 1 748 544 B ≈ 1.7 MiB), but what the install really costs is the tree with its dependencies: 313 672 155 B and 461 758 222 B, about 160× and 264× the figure shown, because the adapters pull the agent's own SDK (@anthropic-ai/claude-agent-sdk 0.3.300; @openai/codex ^0.160.1). Input from the 22.4 walk (2026-10-19), for the wizard's "package, pinned version and size shown":

The ACP probe's catalogue carries `unpackedBytes`, the package's own `dist.unpackedSize` from the registry. That figure is the package alone; the install's real cost is its dependency tree, measured on this machine after the walk's install (`du -sb`):

- @agentclientprotocol/claude-agent-acp 0.93.0: 1 956 577 B in the catalogue (1.9 MiB) → 313 672 155 B installed, of which its node_modules 311 715 578 B (@anthropic-ai/claude-agent-sdk 0.3.300, @agentclientprotocol/sdk 1.9.0, diff 9.0.0, zod 4.6.7). About 160× the figure shown.

- The two together: 775 430 377 B.

Both installed without root with `npm install -g --prefix ~/.local @agentclientprotocol/claude-agent-acp@0.93.0 @agentclientprotocol/codex-acp@2.2.2` (1 min 21 s, 133 packages); the walk's full record is the 22.4 walk comment. title: The unit machine's guards are never sent the event they exist to refuse, so a guard that always passed would go unnoticed
description:
What happens: in `src/fill/fsm.ts` 32 distinct guard predicates survive a mutant that makes them always pass (`ConditionalExpression -> true`), and so do the comparisons and `||` rewrites on the same lines (180, 186, 190, 202, 206, 210, 214, 218, 222, 226, 230, 231, 235, 240, 241, 243, 247, 251, 255, 259, 277, 287, 297, 492, 498, 502, 514, 522, 530, 534, 687, 688). `test/fill-fsm.test.ts` walks each transition's accepted path, and its refusal table covers the fence, generation, retry-count and cause guards, so the rest are only ever seen holding.
What should happen: one test per guard that sends the event the guard refuses, in the state where that event is offered, and asserts the transition was not taken and the refusal names that guard — `generation-current`, `cause-budget-exhausted`, `named(configuration)`, `nothingInFlight(evidence)`, `event.children.every(...)` with one child failing, `retryAt` exactly equal to `context.retryAt`, `fence` equal to `context.fence`.
What would disprove it: that test failing to kill its mutant, or a guard shown unreachable from every state that offers its event (then it is dead code and belongs to the table's removal, not to a test).
Where it came from: the stage's mutation sample (StrykerJS 9.6.1 over src/fill/fsm.ts 1-738 against test/fill-fsm.test.ts, 998 mutants, 86.55-93.94 % per chunk): report /tmp/madarch-stage19-mutation/report.md.

title: The machine-table refusals of fsm-core are never asserted, so a declaration fault would pass as a working table
description:
What happens: in `src/fill/fsm-core.ts` twenty `if (condition) raise(...)` refusals survive a mutant that removes them (lines 47, 49, 180, 181, 190, 192, 193, 194, 215, 218, 219, 222, 285, 287, 292, 301, 306, 312, 315, 370): no states declared, an initial state not among them, a transition id declared twice, a transition leaving or entering an unknown state, an empty event, an action or guard without a description, states no transition reaches, a non-atomic target, an effect list that does not match, and a message that cannot be located.
What should happen: a test per refusal that builds the faulty declaration and asserts the thrown message names the file, the line and the fault, in the style `test/fill-fsm.test.ts` already uses for the accepted path. Two pairs may stand behind each other (192/193 behind 181, 306 behind 301); a probe that removes one guard and sees the other still refuse them settles that first.
What would disprove it: a refusal shown unreachable behind an earlier one, which then is redundancy worth removing rather than a test.
Where it came from: the same mutation sample (src/fill/fsm-core.ts 1-373, 352 mutants, 64.49-64.73 %).

What happens: `stage.after ?? []` (line 256) and `adjacency.get(edge.from) ?? []` (line 265) in `src/fill/registry.ts` survive a mutant that fills the fallback, because no test declares an `after` edge the capability graph does not produce, and none is placed by an optional consume alone.
What should happen: a stage declaring `after` with an edge the capability graph does not produce, and a stage whose `consumes.optional` entry is the only thing that places it in the order.
Where it came from: the stage's mutation sample, finding F7.

title: The built-graph clash test sits on a five-second budget its own work does not fit
description:
What happens: `test/server-graphs.test.ts`, "a store that brings a clash into a built two-source graph drops its engine, and the next use refuses instead of answering with duplicate rows", times out at its 5000 ms budget while its neighbours in the same file take 2.9-4.0 s: CI shard 2 of run 39171437383 failed on it, the same SHA passed on the rerun, and on a SkyPilot pod it failed at 5529 ms with three more timeouts in the same file. The test builds two PGlite histories, a two-source graph, then applies a store and rebuilds.
What should happen: the test's own budget raised to what its work costs on a loaded machine (or the work made smaller), so a red shard means a defect rather than a slow runner.
What would disprove it: repeated runs of the file on a loaded machine staying under the budget.
Where it came from: the acceptance of stage madarch-tzte.19; the pod run's record is in /tmp/madarch-stage19-mutation/report.md.

comments.author: claude-coordinator
comments.text:
Owner decision 2026-10-19 ~10:00 MSK («Да»), the first-fill wizard and agent adapters:
1. madarch finds the installed agents (claude, codex, omp, …) and whether the person is logged in to each; the person picks one. Beside them there is always an API-key option for those who do not want to spend a subscription's limits.
2. When the chosen agent needs an ACP adapter (Claude Code: @agentclientprotocol/claude-agent-acp; Codex: @agentclientprotocol/codex-acp), madarch offers to install it with one confirmation, showing package, version and size; it installs into its own folder (~/madarch/agents/<agent>), never globally and never as root; the version is pinned and moves with madarch.
3. madarch never handles the person's credentials: the agent does its own login. The wizard says plainly that a fill spends the plan's limits or credit.
4. The adapters are not bundled inside the madarch binary: the Claude adapter is built on the Claude Agent SDK under Anthropic's terms; the person fetches it from npm on those terms.
Context: Anthropic's Agent SDK docs bar third-party products from offering claude.ai login or rate limits without approval; local madarch driving the agent the person installed and logged in to themselves does neither (owner, same conversation).

description:

- madarch fill [--agent claude|codex] [--max-units N] in a product folder starts (or resumes) a run over the product's connected repositories: inventory, index, claims and code map, synthesis, question review where available; pages land on the agent branch madarch/fill/<run-id>, one commit per stage, merged into the default branch when no human edit conflicts.

title: Let an agent write the intended model of a repository
description:
A skill for coding agents that reads a repository with the agent's own tools (the language's import graph, contract and schema files) and by reading it (README, architecture documents, code), and writes the intended-model YAML inside the repository. title: Check a repository's intended model against the repository
description:
Stage 1 of madarch-utk (change agent-model): the evidence format with commit and blob, and the model check (docs/changes/agent-model/capabilities/model-check.md).

## Done when
The model check, run from a checkout of madarch on a git repository, meets every scenario of model-check and intended-model/evidence in docs/changes/agent-model/ through tests over repositories the tests build with git (a squash-merged commit included); run by hand on a small repository it prints errors, stale items and problems with their methods and renders the views into a folder; bun run check, bun test, bun run schemas and bun run views reproduce the committed files; mutation and a different-model review pass.

title: The wiki opens on a start page for the reader's role: product manager, architect, newcomer, owner
description:
Idea from the owner, 2026-10-14 ~23:55 MSK, after comparing madarch with Google Code Wiki, DeepWiki and Hermes code-wiki, Wiki Architect, the LLM Wiki Schema and product-architect. The owner doubted whether madarch is needed over code-only wikis; the agreed position: keep the core (intent linked to code across repositories, checked) and fix the value a person gets in the first minutes. Taken up after the standalone milestone's wiki-usable work, not into the current slice.

Each role gets a start page of what it needs first, from the same graph: a product manager the goals, state and gaps; an architect the parts, links and decisions; a newcomer where to begin and the path to the part they need; an owner where the product stands against its vision. The roles and what each page gathers are product data (manifest), not engine data. Reference: Wiki Architect's persona onboarding (contributor, staff engineer, executive, product manager); the vision's audience list.

Would show it is worth it: a reader of a given role answers their first question without using the sidebar.
Left out: access control by role.
